newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy opposition calls budget a rainstorm of taxes.
newsitem.headline: Italy opposition calls budget a rainstorm of taxes.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi defended his government's tough 1997 budget on Saturday from a barrage of criticism by opposition and business leaders who branded the package a "rainstorm of taxes".
Prodi's cabinet approved the budget after an 11-hour marathon meeting on Friday, vowing it would put Italy among the first wave of nations founding a single European currency.

"The truth was we had a precise goal: calculate what it would take to be part of Europe and then take our decision," Prodi told reporters at a business conference in the northern town of Piacenza on Saturday.
"We couldn't worry whether this (decision) would provoke complaints or disappointment," he added.

But the budget, which will cut 62.5 trillion lire ($41.12 billion) off next year's deficit, did just that as opposition and business leaders slammed the government for raising taxes and failing to cut pension and healthcare benefits.

Centre-right leader Silvio Berlusconi called the budget "a rainstorm of taxes that will only worsen the exasperation of tax payers, especially in the north, and render even more desperate the situation of the unemployed in the south".
Berlusconi, a former prime minister, said the austere measures would only worsen an economy that was already on the verge of recession, echoing a view voiced by some analysts.
"We needed a budget aimed at development, not one further pushing us towards recession," he said in a statement.

The government said the heart of the budget was worth 37.5 trillion lire ($24.7 billion), with 25 trillion lire ($16.4 billion) coming from planned spending cuts and 12.5 trillion lire ($8.2 billion) from fresh revenues.

In addition, the government intends to raise 13 trillion lire from a special "Euro Tax" and 12 trillion lire from so far unspecified "treasury operations". Both measures will be fully elaborated before the end of the year.
The government had said it is counting on the central bank to cut interest rates, thus helping reduce the cost of borrowing money in time to make up for the fiscal tightening.
Employers' association Confindustria said praised the government's austerity efforts but criticised the package for failing to make structual changes to pensions and healthcare.

"An important opportunity has been lost to correct structural imbalances in pension and healthcare spending which will, in any case, need to be reduced if Italy wants to remain in the European Union," said Confindustria head Giorgio Fossa.

The government shelved plans to tax pensions and raise charges for hospital treatment after the hard left Communist Refoundation party's leader, Fausto Bertinotti, threatened to scupper the budget in parliament.
The centre-left government relies on support from the Marxist-inspired party in the lower house Chamber of Deputies.
Pierferdinando Casini, leader of a small Roman Catholic party allied with Berlusconi, said the government had been held hostage on the budget bill by Communist Refoundation.
"Bertinotti is the great victor here and it would be an act of coherence for him to take part in the government now," Casini told reporters in the central city of Bologna.
Prodi, pointing to the positive reaction financial markets have had to the budget, rejected such criticism as unfounded.
"If this is being defined as 'Bertinotti's budget', then why did Wall Street like it so much?" Prodi asked?
"Evidently something is wrong in such a judgment."

Italian bond markets and the lira have soared in recent days on a tidal wave of optimism over Italy's chances of meeting strict qualifying criteria for membership of European economic and monetary union (EMU) by 1999.

The budget, which parliament must approve by the end of December, aims to reduce Italy's deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) ratio to three percent by the end of next year, putting Italy on course to join the countries that establish a single European currency in 1999. ($1=1,520 Lire)
